clinical_record:
A 70‐year‐old woman with an undifferentiated connective tissue disorder and rheumatoid arthritis was treated with hydroxychloroquine in 2010, after which she developed a severe generalized bullous and pustular rash that resolved over three months following drug discontinuation and corticosteroid therapy. In 2022, hydroxychloroquine was restarted for her rheumatoid arthritis. Three days after restarting the drug, she was admitted with widespread erythema, desquamation, and pustulation. She denied any history of psoriasis. Laboratory studies revealed marked leukocytosis, hyperglycemia, hypoproteinemia, transaminitis, and an elevated C‐reactive protein level. Skin biopsies from the back demonstrated separation of the stratum corneum with multifocal subcorneal collections of neutrophils, underlying spongiotic epidermis with neutrophilic exocytosis, papillary dermal edema, and a superficial perivascular and interstitial infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, histiocytes, neutrophils, and rare eosinophils.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

candidate_registry.label: Drug Rash with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms

A 34-year-old Filipino man presented with a 4-month history of left eye proptosis, diplopia, and chemosis without epistaxis, headache, or nasal obstruction. Endoscopic nasal examination revealed a mass at the level of the left middle turbinate extending into the left nasal roof and eroding the upper nasal septum. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed mild left proptosis with full extraocular movements, no papilledema, and normal visual acuity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated an expansile, mildly enhancing soft-tissue mass in the anterosuperior nasal cavity encroaching on the left orbital cavity, with remodeling of the left medial orbital wall and extension to the level of the cribriform plate, along with retention of secretions in the left frontal sinus. MRI (T1-weighted postcontrast) showed an enhancing mass reaching the nasal vault without dural enhancement or intracranial extension; T2 and non–contrast T1 sequences revealed no intratumoral hemorrhage or cystic change. The patient underwent endoscopic endonasal resection, which disclosed a cystic mass occupying the left fronto-ethmoid region with destruction of the anterior skull base and erosion of the left lamina papyracea; the dura was exposed but intact, and no cerebrospinal fluid leak was noted. A routine functional endoscopic sinus surgery was completed after tumor excision.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of abnormal behavior, decreased concentration, and postural instability. She had a history of insomnia and irritable bowel syndrome and was taking vitamin D3, vitamin K, manganese, and activated charcoal. She and her parents denied other medications. She had been started on lorazepam by her general practitioner without improvement.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Teeth had a greyish discoloration. Neurologic exam showed confusion, impaired attention, and disorientation. Muscle tone and strength were normal; coordination, sensation, and cranial nerves were intact; there were no pyramidal signs.

While in the emergency department, she became more somnolent and developed frequent myoclonic jerks. Laboratory tests including CBC, renal, hepatic, and thyroid function, CRP, vitamin B12, and folate were normal; syphilis and HIV tests were negative. Noncontrast brain CT was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture showed protein 47 mg/dL (15–45) and 10 WBC/μL (<5). Empiric IV acyclovir and ceftriaxone were started for possible infectious encephalitis.

On the neurology service, she remained moderately drowsy with exuberant generalized myoclonus at rest and on action. EEG revealed generalized background slowing without focal or periodic features. Brain MRI on hospital day 5 was normal. She clinically worsened despite antivirals and antibiotics, so intravenous immunoglobulin was given empirically for presumed autoimmune encephalitis. A trial of levetiracetam 1000 mg/day failed to improve the myoclonus.

A man in his 50s presented with new and progressive satellite lesions while undergoing pembrolizumab therapy. Two years earlier, he had undergone a wide local excision with graft repair for a left posterior auricular scalp lesion. An incidentally resected lymph node was found to be focally involved, with no evidence of distant metastatic disease. Within months, multiple unresectable satellite lesions appeared. He received 4 cycles of ipilimumab, followed by a second wide local excision when new lesions appeared. Additional satellite lesions developed and he began pembrolizumab therapy, but after 5 cycles, local progression occurred in the satellite lesions.

Multiple satellite lesions were present on the left posterior auricular scalp area. After treatment, clinically regressed lesions with persistent black pigmentation were noted.

A 67‐year‐old man with a 3‐year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin, glimepiride, and a prior percutaneous coronary intervention for acute myocardial infarction 2 months earlier was referred for treatment of newly diagnosed extensive ulcerative colitis. He had a 40‐year smoking history but had quit after his myocardial infarction. He reported four episodes of bloody diarrhea daily but denied abdominal pain or fever. On admission for a 2‐week educational trial of a plant‐based diet, his body weight was 69 kg and physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed normal white‐cell count, bilirubin, and liver function tests. Ten days after admission, plasma glucose rose from 258 mg/dL to 449 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c increased from 7.3% to 8.0%. Urinalysis showed no proteinuria but microalbuminuria of 50.7 mg/day. Anti–glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies were negative. Both serum amylase and lipase were elevated. Contrast‐enhanced CT and MR cholangiopancreatography demonstrated swelling of the pancreas with a peripheral rim and slight narrowing of the main pancreatic duct. Serum IgG4 was 36.0 mg/dL (reference range, 4.5–117 mg/dL).

An 18-year-old Chinese woman noted a grey dot in the central vision of her left eye 4 days before presentation. She had a known plexiform neurofibroma of the arm confirmed by biopsy 1 year earlier; otherwise, she denied medical history, trauma, family history, smoking, coffee, tea, illicit drugs, or oral contraceptive use. Blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg. Visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye, with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Slit-lamp examination showed mild subcapsular cataracts bilaterally. Automated perimetry revealed a small central scotoma in the left eye. Fundus examination demonstrated a swollen optic disc in the right eye and, in the left eye, a parafoveal grey-white deep retinal lesion and a cotton-wool spot in the posterior pole. Fluorescein angiography showed a focal retinal filling defect corresponding to the cotton-wool spot and hypofluorescence without leakage at the right optic disc. Swept-source optical coherence tomography of the left macula revealed hyperreflective bands in the inner nuclear layer consistent with paracentral acute middle maculopathy. Carotid Doppler ultrasound and transthoracic echocardiography were normal. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count with differential, liver enzymes, renal function, lipid profile, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, blood glucose, hemoglobin A1C, antinuclear antibody, anti–double-stranded DNA antibody, anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, syphilis serology, HIV, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, angiotensin-converting enzyme, and tests for protein C, protein S, antithrombin III, and homocystinuria, were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance angiography of the brain was normal. Brain MRI with and without contrast showed bilateral vestibular schwannomas, a parasellar mass consistent with a meningioma, and a cervical extramedullary lesion. Orbital CT showed normal optic nerve contours and calcified lesions in the right temporal lobe.

A 25-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a 1-month history of insidious-onset right lower abdominal pain. She also had lifelong non-pitting edema of the left leg extending to the labia majora. She was otherwise healthy, with regular menses and no tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, she was afebrile, blood pressure was 110/80 mmHg, pulse 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiac and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic exam was normal. Abdomen revealed a firm, non-tender, mobile mass measuring approximately 12 cm × 10 cm in the right lower quadrant; bimanual pelvic examination confirmed a right adnexal mass.  

Baseline hematologic, biochemical, thyroid, renal, and HIV/HBV/HCV serologies were within normal limits. Tumor markers were all in the reference range: carcinoembryonic antigen 1.14 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase 251 U/L, α-fetoprotein 2.16 ng/mL, CA-125 21 U/mL, and β-hCG 2.39 µIU/mL. Pap smear was negative.  

Transvaginal ultrasound showed multiple uterine fibroids and a large hypoechoic lesion in the right adnexa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a well-marginated thin-walled solid-cystic lesion measuring 16.1 × 7.9 × 8.1 cm in the abdominopelvic region containing a 2.3 × 2.1 cm cystic component and a 5.8 × 5.7 cm solid component. A separate 7 × 3.2 × 2.8 cm cystic lesion was noted in the right parauterine region. Bilateral ovaries were not visualized separately. The uterus was bulky with multiple fibroids. Multiple small mesenteric lymph nodes were seen. Incidentally, a double inferior vena cava was identified, with the left cava draining via the left renal vein to the right-sided cava. Serology for filarial infection was negative.  

Although tumor markers were normal, the imaging findings were concerning for an ovarian neoplasm. A staging laparotomy with surgical excision was planned, with a provisional diagnosis of a malignant ovarian tumor in the setting of uterine fibroids and unilateral lymphedema.

A 62-year-old woman presented with 4 months of soreness, swelling, and limited movement of her right palm and wrist. Six months earlier, she had been stabbed by a fishbone. She had been diagnosed with a tenosynovial giant cell tumor by MRI at a local hospital and treated with traditional Chinese medicine, but her symptoms worsened over the past 2 months. She denied respiratory symptoms, skin disorders, recent travel, or tuberculosis exposure and had no family history of inflammatory arthritis or psoriasis. On examination, there was swelling, tenderness, and limited motion of the right palm and fingers without percussion pain or bone friction. Physiological reflexes were intact. Laboratory studies showed normal leukocyte count, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; rheumatoid factor was negative. Noncontrast MRI of the right hand demonstrated patchy abnormal signal around the deep flexor tendons and carpal canal, with hypointense signals on T1-weighted imaging and hyperintense signals on proton-density fat-suppressed sequences. Post-contrast images demonstrated homogeneous enhancement of the tendons and synovial membrane, supporting synovial hyperplasia, while diffusion-weighted imaging and ADC maps suggested restricted diffusion. The median nerve was mildly compressed and deformed, and degenerative changes were noted in some carpal bones. Ultrasonography showed rough, thickened bone surfaces and decreased echogenicity at the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints and along multiple flexor tendons, with peripheral and internal flow on color Doppler. The flexor retinaculum was elevated, and the median nerve was flattened at the carpal canal. Based on these findings, preliminary diagnoses included degenerative arthritis, synovitis, tenosynovitis, and atypical carpal tunnel syndrome; a neoplastic lesion remained in the differential.

A 62-year-old man presented with a two-week history of an asymptomatic swelling in the right lower half of the face and reduced mouth opening. He reported two prior similar episodes over eight years: the first, five years ago, was treated as a buccal-space infection with incision and drainage; the second, two years ago, resolved spontaneously. He had no pain or fever and was a known diabetic on regular medication. 

On examination, there was gross right facial asymmetry. Extraorally, a 6 × 6 cm ovoid subcutaneous swelling extended from the level of the right lateral canthus to 1 cm below the corner of the mouth and from the corner of the mouth posteriorly to the mandibular ramus. The borders were ill-defined, the consistency ranged from soft to firm, and the overlying skin was normal. There was no lymphadenopathy, paresthesia, or facial palsy. Intraorally, the right buccal mucosa was elevated and glistening, with no vestibular obliteration; mouth opening was restricted by the mass.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the face showed a well-defined soft-tissue mass with cystic areas in the right buccal space. Intracystic loculations with dense cystic content were noted, and there was erosion of the posterior buccal cortex without perforation of the maxilla; the maxillary antrum was compressed.

A clinical diagnosis of a nonspecific chronic abscess with buccal-space involvement was made. Under general anesthesia, an intraoral approach was used to excise the lesion in toto with a margin of fibrous tissue. The lesion shelled out easily, with no involvement of buccinator muscle or bone. The excised specimen measured 4.8 × 4.5 cm, was creamish-brown, firm, irregular, and had a leathery pouch-like appearance, entirely within the soft tissue of the buccal space.

A 70-year-old Japanese man presented with dysphagia and was diagnosed with T3N0M0 esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 6.6%), percutaneous coronary intervention, and radiotherapy for laryngeal cancer. He underwent two courses of 5-fluorouracil/docetaxel/cisplatin and then thoracoscopic esophagectomy with retrosternal gastric tube reconstruction and cervical esophagogastrostomy.

On postoperative day 4, cervical wound erythema with pus and saliva discharge appeared; drainage and intravenous tazobactam/piperacillin were initiated. Despite nutritional support and improved albumin levels, a refractory anastomotic fistula persisted, and Enterobacter cloacae was cultured from the wound. On day 60, salvage reconstruction with a free jejunal autograft and pectoralis major muscle flap coverage was performed.

Fifteen days after reconstruction, he developed worsening low back pain and fever (38.2 °C). Examination revealed lumbar spinal tenderness and bilateral leg weakness without sensory loss. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 9200/µL and C-reactive protein of 9.86 mg/dL. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. Blood cultures grew Enterobacter cloacae. MRI of the lumbar spine demonstrated decreased T1 signal and increased T2 and STIR signal at L4–L5.

A 35-year-old West African man with no prior psychiatric or medical history presented to clinic with a 1-week history of escalating behavioral changes. His family reported episodes of talkativeness, incoherent speech, visual and auditory hallucinations, insomnia, and grandiose and persecutory delusions. He denied head injury, substance use, or stressors and had no family history of psychiatric illness. He worked as a mechanical engineer in a mining community with potential mercury exposure and had no systemic or respiratory symptoms despite known community spread of COVID-19.

On examination he was afebrile, BP 135/80 mmHg, pulse 88 bpm, and with normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation. General and neurologic exams were unremarkable. He appeared disheveled, restless, and agitated but was oriented to time, place, and person. Speech was loud and clear without latency. He exhibited circumstantial thought, grandiose delusions (“I am a prophet of God”), persecutory delusions, and both auditory (“gunshots”) and visual (a mob) hallucinations. Memory was intact and he had no insight.

Laboratory studies showed a normal CBC, renal function, and albumin; γ‐glutamyl transferase was elevated at 81 IU/L (normal < 55) and total bilirubin 26 μmol/L (normal 3.4–20.5). Malaria and typhoid screens were negative. Urinalysis revealed transient proteinuria and glycosuria that normalized on repeat. Head CT scan was normal. A lateral flow COVID-19 antigen test and confirmatory RT-PCR were both positive.

A 60-year-old man with hypertension and Parkinson’s disease presented with 3 months of progressive lower extremity edema and acute onset of altered mental status. On admission, he was somnolent and disoriented; examination showed symmetric lower extremity edema, hepatomegaly, and ascites without stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory tests revealed AST 3877 U/L, ALT 2939 U/L, total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dL, INR 3.8, white blood cell count 19.4×10^3/μL, platelets 63×10^3/μL, lactic acid 13.9 mmol/L, BUN 67 mg/dL, creatinine 3.3 mg/dL, with a negative acetaminophen level and toxicology screen. Viral hepatitis panels, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and HIV testing were negative. A diagnostic paracentesis was negative for infection or malignancy. Tests for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, hemochromatosis, and Wilson’s disease were unremarkable. The patient developed hepatorenal syndrome requiring continuous venovenous hemofiltration.  
Lower-extremity Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated extensive bilateral femoral–popliteal and iliac vein thrombosis. IVC filter placement was aborted due to clot burden. Hepatic ultrasonography with Doppler showed hepatic vein thrombosis and reversal of portal venous flow. Contrast CT of the abdomen, thorax, and pelvis revealed thrombus extending into the right atrium. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a large echodense mass in the right atrium with preserved left ventricular function. Cardiac MRI demonstrated a 10.6×5.0×5.6-cm heterogeneous pericardial mass invading the right atrium.
